Uniform Title: Parākramapūjā Manuscript:

Last part of NGMCP manuscript no. 5-4656 Reel No.: A 175/11 Description: Description by Mark S.G. Dyczkowski: This manuscript contains the concluding portion of the ritual manual for the worship of the deity Parākrama. It details the final stages of the liturgical procedure, including the concluding offerings, the recitation of specific mantras, and the rites of dissolution (*pratisaṃhāra*) and benediction (*svasti-vācana*). The text is written in Nevārī script and provides instructions for the officiant regarding the visualization (*dhyāna*) and the sequence of gestures (*mudrā*) associated with the deities of the *parākrama* cycle. It concludes with the formal dismissal of the deities and the distribution of the ritual remains.

The text, which remains unnamed, is copied from a manuscript that begins with *Aśeṣakulavallarī*. I have titled it *Parākramapūjā*. It informs us that it belongs to the tradition known as the *Aśeṣāmbhavīmata*. [It concerns] the Goddess Parā.

Worshipped here, she is also called Nityā. The worship occurs both internally and externally. The internal processes are described in detail. As is customary, the focus remains on the flows of the vital force (*prāṇa*) and the *Kuṇḍalinī*. [The offering of] wine and other [substances...]

The details confirm the Kaula character of the external worship. The text provides an extensive and numerous array of mantras, from which its close association with the Śrīvidyā school is evident, even though the śrīcakra is not the object of worship.

1a) Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva.
Aiṃ 5. Salutations to Caṇḍikā.
Salutation to Gaṇapati.
I perpetually bow to her who resembles a mass of lightning, whose form is subtle as the peak of a mountain, who has pierced through the three *liṅgas* with a body like a broken lotus fiber, and who,
having ascended above the portion of emission (*visarga*) to the *akula*, is the essence of the stream of nectar.

Salutations forever to that eternal one, whose supreme Kaulika Śakti consists of the liquefied essence of molten coral, and whose lotus feet are worshipped by gods, asuras, serpents, and others, as well as by lords of sages, siddhas, and kinnaras.

I bow to the supreme Goddess Nityā, who is seated upon the throne of the syllable *aiṃ*, who is the sky, the creeper of delusion, the eternal one, and the bestower of boons both eternal and non-eternal.
The Goddess said:
O Blessed One, Lord of the gods of gods, Bhairava, destroyer of worldly existence!
O Lord of gods, I desire to hear the definitive exposition of the Tripura mantra.
The Great Lotus Forest, endowed with the three genders,
as well as the Kadamba-golaka and especially the Brahma-randhra.
Tell me in the seventh [chapter] about that which is joined with the five mudrās, endowed with the three seats (pīṭhas), and the distinction between Kula and Akula.
The illustrious Bhairava said:
The linga facing west is proclaimed to be situated in the yoni;
the stream of bindus from the heart to the head is the self-existent expression of the bāṇa.
The other [letter] situated in the interval, as well as the Visarga and the letter Ṭha,
and the Mahāpadma-dhana— these are proclaimed here as the Yoga-pīṭha.
That desire, in the form of a drop (bindu), has the shape of a *kadamba* bud;
right there is the aperture of Brahma (*brahmarandhra*), the mandala that is the support of the *suṣumnā*.
The principles beginning with Earth are indeed the designators of the mudrās;
the principle called Pūrṇa, which is of the nature of the Bindu, resides between the two bows.
Above that is Vāmā; then the garden is Guṇabheda;
Kāmarūpa becomes Śakti, which is declared to be Visarga, O Dear One.
One should correctly visualize a great thousand-spoked lotus with red filaments and a cool [center],
situated there, raining down drops of blood.
I shall now explain the binding of that mudrā previously indicated, which is known as the Secret and has the nature of nectar, by means of which one attains the state of a servant.
At the outset, having joined the mind with the previous yoga,
one should practice the vow while contracting the vulva located between the anus and the genitals.
Having meditated upon Kāma, who has entered a revolving womb, resembling a bandhūka flower,
like the blazing fire of time, and possessing a radiance equal to ten million flashes of lightning;
Above that, however, is the subtle crest (śikhā), which is the digit of Ramā belonging to Vidrūpa;
one should contemplate oneself as being united with it, having become one.
They proceed by way of the path of Brahmā through the sequence of piercing the *liṅga*,
[reaching that state] which resembles ten million suns and is as cool as ten million moons.
The nectar situated within the emission, characterized by supreme bliss, is melted,
enriched with the radiant luster of blood, and pours forth as a continuous stream.
Having drunk the divine nectar of the *kula*, one should enter the *kula* once again;
one enters the *akula* once more through the yoga of the *mātrā*, and not otherwise.
And she is designated as *prāṇa* within this supreme Lord's tantra;
for she is drawn forth from *vidyā* until she reaches the end of *prāṇa*, when she is touched.
For him who is supremely devoted to that [practice], day by day,
he is liberated from the bondage of existence through the sufferings of old age, death, and the like.
The fourfold creation proceeds from the womb;
it dissolves again into that [womb], beginning with the fire of time (kālāgni) and ending with Śiva.
The supreme Yonimudrā is rightly proclaimed as its essential reality;
by the mere state of being its great consort, what else could she be on this earth?
O Goddess of gods, he who worships with a spell or alters the mantra is not successful; this is the truth, the truth again and again.
Those mantras which have been severed, those that have grown old, those that are paralyzed, those that are firmly pinned down, as well as those that are burnt,
those that are emaciated, those that are defiled, and those that are thus described;
Sealed and filled with intoxication, they were rendered as if in deep sleep;
likewise, the children, the old, and the mature women proud of their youth [were affected].
2a) But those who stand on the side of the enemies— devoid of virtue,
lacking limbs, destitute, and cut into hundreds of pieces— [are not to be killed].
When these [mantras] are joined with this *vicenā*,
they all become bestowers of supernatural powers (*siddhi*) and liberation (*mokṣa*) in no time at all, provided they are employed by a teacher (*deśika*).
If a mantra, whether auspicious or inauspicious, is recited in the form of its constituent letters, there it succeeds; that Māyā is [mastered] by means of the *ādiyoni* mudrā, and not otherwise.
O Goddess of the Gods, having initiated [the disciple] according to the rule and having consecrated him a thousandfold, one should then transform the body within this Tantra; it cannot be otherwise.
Even if one were to kill the inhabitants of the three worlds or commit a thousand murders of Brahmins, one is not stained by those sins through the practice of the Yonimudrā.

Having gratified [the deity] over a long period through the arrangement of mudrās and maṇḍalas, as well as recitation, fire-offerings, vows, and so forth, and having recognized his unwavering devotion;
Having understood his inclination toward renunciation, one should not reveal that [teaching] to him;
rather, O Goddess, at whatever time the rays of the Goddess [shine forth], [then one should teach].
And [it is] glorious, free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*), eternal, and the true nature of that which is beyond perception.
[Salutation] to the one whose body is entirely unstained, the self who is the creator of all,
the agent, the enjoyer, the destroyer, the ordainer, and the one of immeasurable power.
She was born from the *chāta-pharoja* of that supreme vital force (*śūṣma*), which is the ultimate reality and possesses a body;
she is the mother whose form is the five elements.
For those who follow the lineage, the union with the effect arises as either one or sixfold;
likewise, there is the Supreme Will, the Knower, the one called Action, and Kuṇḍalinī.
The Mātṛkā is said to be the sixtieth; it is considered praised as the supreme division.
In the beginning is the Supreme (Parā) with the fourfold [set], and in the second is the fifth, which is Icchā.
The third is threefold, the knower is one, the fourth is sevenfold, and the third is threefold.
The fifth is Kuṇḍalī, considered the eightfold Veda-mātṛkā;
from Parā she is born as Icchā, and she abides on the path of space.
2b) Thirty-six leaders are said to reside in the region of the throat;
from the Will [of the Goddess] the Knower arises, and she is considered to be Vāgīśvarī.
The twenty-seven leaders are supported by the Unstruck (anāhata);
the Knower, born of action, is considered the Śaiva Vahnīśvarī.
The thirty-first leader is situated in Maṇipūra;
she is known as Kuṇḍalīlātā, and she is the leader.
The one known as the twenty-sixth leader is said to be based upon the self-consecration (svādhiṣṭhāna);
she is called Mātṛkā, arising from Kuṇḍalī, and the remainder is considered to be Pṛthvīśvarī.
The Mistress of the Twenty-eight is also supported by the sphere of jaggery;
she, the Mistress, is likewise divided individually by the command of Śambhu.
Thus, the rays of Śambhu number exactly three hundred and sixty;
they are further accompanied by the six powers beginning with Yava and the six guardians.
They say there are three hundred and seventy-two [names] of Vipaschit;
by the mere recollection of them, one may wander the earth as one liberated while living.
If one is unable to remember all [the deities], one should remember even a single one among these six.
The light arising from remembering these destroys sin, and it arises even more so from their worship.
Whether through meditation on Lakṣmī or as one liberated while living, I abide in this lineage;
in the field of these three is the seat (pīṭha) called Prayoga, which is both supreme and non-supreme.
The tree is the seat of these three; the body is the seat of the three [others]; and the head is said to be the seat of the months.
In the tree, there is for them the creeper called Mleccha, consisting of accumulated [defilements];
furthermore, for others, the mind is joined with the five non-causes.
Therefore, through victory over that, the fruit of all sequential worship shall arise;
it is known as the glorious seat of Śrī, and from that, the five elements indeed emerge.
"The sixth is the nature of *ājñā*, which is like the source of the five"—
thus it is stated even in the venerable *Aṅka*.
O gods, one who worships Parākrama obtains that very fruit which is attained by worshipping the five ancestors; this is the truth.
"He in whom the Krama has reached the throat and proceeds correctly is himself the Blessed Lord Śambhu"— this is the teaching of the venerable Śāmbhavīmata.
Therefore, with every effort and according to the sequence that will be explained,
one should worship the Bhairava-krama constantly for the sake of both worldly enjoyment and liberation.

Having risen in the morning, one who is peaceful should [meditate] upon Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and the others, together with the six Pretas, within the thousand-petaled lotus of the skull (varāṭaka) that contains gold.
In the center of the pericarp of the lotus, at the end of the twelve [fingers],
one should recollect the three words according to the instruction of the Guru, preceded by the remembrance of the Guru.
Red, white, and mixed—these are indeed the secrets above the *preta*;
they assume forms at will, born from the two feet.
One should likewise meditate upon the God and Goddess, as well as the Lord, each joined with their respective mantra; one should contemplate the Guru, the wife of the Guru, and the Goddess of gods.
O Lord of the World, whatever I do from morning until evening, and from evening until the next morning, let that be an act of worship unto You.
Having first offered this prayer and bowed to the sandals of the Guru,
he should go outside; then, having reached a pure place not far away,
he should perform the purification and sipping of water (ācamana) and so forth.
Having performed the gargling and used the tooth-stick, and having remained silent, the wise man should bathe and perform the twilight devotions according to the prescribed rule.
The method of bathing is twofold, distinguished as external and internal;
O Pārvatī, the internal bath occurs within the heart.
I shall speak concerning your enemies and the five groups of adversaries as well.
Then, reflecting upon the inner bath, he remembered that which flows from the midst of the three feet [of the Lord],
whose power is Being-Consciousness-Bliss (saccidānanda), and who is the object of contemplation;
for yogis, liberation is attained through mere remembrance.
3b) One should meditate upon oneself as being bathed by that [water] for the sake of the pacification of existence (bhava).
Thereafter, one should meditate on the protection [of others] according to one's capacity.
Another is the river consisting of non-attachment, and another is the river whose nature is awakening;
in the middle is another consisting of truth, whose sole form is knowledge and bliss.
She who consists of all bliss and is indeed the very nature of the Supreme Brahman,
having reached the lotus on the left, flows toward the end of the left foot.
She who is known as the primordial power (Ādi-śakti) whose form is to be cognized, who possesses her own essential nature,
and who, on the right side of the lotus, flows toward the feet as Smṛti.
That river known as Satyarūpā, whose origin is primordial and who possesses her own essential form,
having reached Padmā in the center, flows through the space of the Suṣumṇā.
In the Lakṣmīkulārṇava.
The *iḍā* is renowned as the Gaṅgā, and the *piṅgalā* is the river Yamunā;
Sarasvatī is to be known as being between them—this is remembered as Prayāga.
Since the external bath is fivefold, consisting of the five elements,
therefore, by performing the mantra-bath, all types of bathing are accomplished.
The seed-syllables consisting of the five elements—la, va, ra, ya, ha, and ī, accompanied by the bindu—are placed on the mantra in the right hand over the water.
By joining the hundred fingers of the left hand, one should sprinkle the head;
having filled [the vessel] with the *vāsa-māsikā* mantra, [there arises] water consisting of light in the state of emission (*sṛṣṭi*).
Having first performed the purification of impurities through the right nostril,
and having recited the mantra, one should sprinkle [the water] over the head.
"Arghamarṣa, śametat, hi, śakalāḍhya, viśodhanam"—
thus is the bath, which is the cessation that wards off all evils from the very beginning.
Then, having bathed, the wise man should perform the twilight devotions according to the prescribed rule; by performing the twilight devotions, he attains the fulfillment of dharma, kama, and artha.
Having meditated upon the seed-syllable *tuṃ*, which has a yellow luster, within the four-petalled lotus at the *mūlādhāra*,
one should visualize it flowing three times within the circle of fire (*vahni-maṇḍala*) inside the nostrils.
4a) He has four arms and eyes, shining with a yellowish-white luster like the sun;
he holds a radiant trident and a skull-cup in his hands.
Having thus meditated upon Jyeṣṭhā, who is equal to the rising sun, one should recite the mantra with concentration:
Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ Hsryūṃ Hsauḥ Lhā Hsauṃ Hrauṃ Jyeṣṭhā Saṃdhyāyai Hsauṃḥ Lhoṃ Hsauṃḥ Hkhphreṃ Śrī Hrīṃ Aiṃ Śrī Pādukāṃ Pūjayāmi Tarpayāmi Namaḥ.
Having thus offered the threefold *arghya*, one should recite the *Gāyatrī* mantra a hundred times while focusing on the Sun and other deities situated in the mouth.
Thereafter, in due order, one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*) for Asitāṅga,
Carcika, Yoga, Harasiddhi, and Hāṭaka.
With a concentrated mind, one should worship Kālī, Kālarātrī, Bhīṣaṇa, and the eight Bhairavas, using either water, funeral offerings, or sacrificial oblations.
Knowledge arises from the Virāj for one who is intent upon the Gāyatrī:
"We know the six-faced one; we meditate upon the multi-footed one; may that Rudra inspire us.
This is indeed that which was previously conceived in the center of the solar disc.
One should subsequently join that goddess and her mantra into the root-energy.
Now, for the twilight [ritual] and so forth: having meditated upon the seed-syllable *phoḥ* at the *maṇipūra*, which resembles a dark blue lotus, one should draw it out as before.
[One should meditate on the deity] situated in the middle of the lunar orb, three-eyed and with a dark-blue form.
Having addressed the one mounted on the grandson (pautra), one should likewise [address] the one situated on the left and the other.

And likewise, meditating upon Vāmā bearing [the attributes], one should mutter the mantra: *hrīṃ hsauḥ hrīṃ vāmā saṃdhyāyai hrīṃ hsau hrīṃ* (five times) *śrīpāpūte namaḥ*. Having thus offered the *bhūrava* oblation:
Then, at the evening twilight, having meditated upon the seed-syllable *hrauṃ* of red color at the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, the lotus of the [evening] hour, one should emit [the breath] as before.
4b) She stands in the center of a circle of fire, red in color, and four-armed,
bearing the gesture of fearlessness, a trident, a skull-cup, and likewise a raised index finger.
And on the left side, one should meditate upon Raudrī, who possesses a radiant gaze, is endowed with eyes, and wears various ornaments; having thus meditated, one should recite the mantra.
5 HRAUḤ HSAUḤ HRAUṂ Raudrī Saṃdhyāyai HRAUṂ HSAU HRAUṂ 5 Śrīyāpūta 2.
Having performed the libation as before, one should lead [the deity] back to its own place and cause it to dissolve;
then, having joined that goddess with her mantra, one should unite her within the fundamental radiance (*mūlatejas*).
Thus concludes the procedure for the twilight devotions (saṃdhyā-vidhi).
Now begins the section on expiatory rites (prāyaścitta).
O King, the twilight ritual (saṃdhyā) must indeed be performed as a staircase for Śambhu;
for one who is initiated but devoid of the twilight ritual, there is no fruit of initiation for you.
If one fails to perform the evening *saṃdhyā*, one should recite [the mantra] ten times when it has fallen;
at another time equal to the *saṃdhyā*, one should do so with the *kaṇṭhaka-vidyā* from the Sūtra.
Having performed the ritual with the six-limbed mantra, one should meditate upon that Sautrakaṇḍakī.
Now, meditation.
The Supreme Goddess has six arms, twelve arms, and three eyes;
from the neck upwards she is white in color, while the palms of her hands are yellow.
Extending from the waist down to the feet, she is praised as being nine spans long;
she is sixteen years of age, has reddish limbs, and is adorned with golden ornaments.
Shining with the luster of gold and jewels, she adorns the triple-thousandfold world system;
she who liberates from all sins sits upon a jeweled lion throne.
Above that is white in color, and above that, the white filaments;
situated upon its back is the goddess Trikhaṇḍā, adorned with a garland of jujube fruits.
The Great Goddess, adorned with a jewel crown and blazing with hundreds of divine [rays], filled with joy, and possessing faces that discharge weapons, moves toward the right and bestows grace.
She is the Great Equal One, who has correctly attained that state, who possesses that state, who is partless, and who is the one who goes [to liberation].

5a) Now the mantra: 5 Aiṃ! O you who perform the severance of most difficult deeds, O bestower of boons, O Aghorā, Vicce! O Māyā, who revolves through the three worlds a thousand times, O host of Mothers! Hsrūṃ! 5. This mantra is for the purpose of expiation.
One should recite [the mantra] ten times (10).
Now, at the time of the twilight (saṃdhyā), one should indeed offer [oblations] with the mantra for those who have fallen [from their vows]. Thus, the mental worship of the Sun has been described.
Now follows the worship of the Sun (Saura-pūjā).
One should perform the ritual action with faith, preceded by the recollection of Śrīnātha;
having performed the external purification, one should cleanse the teeth according to the rules.
Having performed the ritual bath with ear-roots and meat, as well as the twilight prayers and libations,
he— purified in soul, free from doubt, and tranquil in mind— performed the Savana sacrifice.
Just as one might enter the clear abode of a householder for worship,
she came there for the sake of that service, accompanied by her entire retinue.
If one desires to see the sun, one should perform sacrifice in its courtyard;
if one possesses ten-fold power, one should perform the *aparopa* [rite] for Mārtaṇḍa.
And so it is stated in the *Nirṇaya*:
"The worship of the Sun is prescribed only for those who possess the fourfold cleverness (*caturatvayi*).
Having reflected upon that, one should perform the worship of the Sun of Consciousness (*cidāditya*) while seated on a comfortable seat."
The wise one should sit facing east on a smooth, even surface,
purified by the ashes of the earth, and restrain his senses.
The general *argha* offering should be performed before oneself, reciting the *praṇava* (oṃ) five times;
the drawing of the mandala should be carried out—this is the common tradition.
Having drawn a hexagon with four *bhūtāṅgula* sides and lower lines,
one should place upon it a vessel that has been purified by mantras along with its support.
Having established [the vessel] and filled it with milk, as well as the waters in the supporting vessels,
one should meditate upon the seed-syllables of Fire, Sun, and Moon, which consist of the mace (gadā).

Having thus performed the ritual for the limbs of that [deity], which consists of the second Praṇava with six long vowels and the syllable *sargha*, one should establish the peaceful [image] on the right.
Having made the vessel common [to all], and having performed the rites up to its installation,
he should worship the second [vessel] with the *nidāna* mantra, honoring it highly with drops.
There, in that general sacrificial pavilion of yoga, one should apply one's own body;
then, one should thoroughly sprinkle all the materials gathered for the solar rite.
While the solar orb was being carried forward by the tip of the horse's nose,
he [anointed it] with musk, sandalwood, and other substances, along with the mantra to be recited.

5 Aiṃ! O you who have the moon, sun, and fire as your womb, cause the attainment of the [four goals of] dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa to flash forth; perform it, perform it! Reveal the great samaya-khecarī-mudrā, reveal it! O you who are clever among those possessing the knowledge of Śambhu, burn away the yellow accomplishment and power, burn them away! Phreṃ kici 2 phreṃ kili 2 phreṃ! O Maṇḍala, O Brahmāṇḍa!
Having worshipped with this mantra— *lasrūṃ mahācaṇḍāśava hseṃ phreṃ* (five times)— one should then draw a circle and an eight-petaled lotus.
Having fashioned a square mandala, one should establish it to the south.
One should draw the general remaining mandala of the offering water (argha) according to the piercing (vedha).
Having prepared a square mandala for the worship with the midday arghya water,
and having established the support, one should perform the worship with this [mantra].
5 Aiṃ, to the seat of the vessel; aiṃ 5.
There, having placed that washed and fumigated vessel, [one should recite]:

*klīṃ* for the general *arghya*, *sauḥ* for the special *arghya*. Thus, having worshipped the *arghya* and the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*), one should bestow power and prosperity upon those who possess the limbs of Śambhu and those who have attained the four states (*caturātman*) by means of the weapon-mantra (*astra*).
Having performed the protective rites (*saṃrakṣā*) and formed the resolve (*saṃkalpa*), one should worship one's own self with the initial [mantras].
Then, in the center of an eight-petaled lotus, one should worship Him who has the form of a *preta* (spirit), lying there; listen to the mantra for that.
5 Aṃ, for Ananta, 5 Aṃ. Having visualized the white Lord of Serpents himself as his own body, with three hoods forming a parasol, one should then worship him.

6a) Beginning from the center, one should worship in the northwest, following the sequence of one’s own *śrīṣukra*. 5 AṂ HŪṂ PHRAṂ to Prabhūtāsana; PHREṂ HŪṂ AṂ 5. In the center: 5 RŪṂ to the Solar Maṇḍala; RAṂ 5 LE to Saura.

Laṃ 5 Śrī 5 Yaṃ Ārādhyāya Yaṃ 5 Śrī 5 Haṃ Paramasukhoya Haṃ 5 Śrī. Thus, in the four corners. Now, the invocation of the maṇḍala: 5 Haṃ. From the center of the vast sky, the seed-syllable Hrauṃ, resembling blood in color, emerging from the nostrils, [invokes] Ananta together with his seat from the corpse.
Having invoked him, one should meditate upon Mārtaṇḍabhairava,
who consists of that seed-syllable, is red in color, possesses a massive body, has six faces, and has hair standing erect.
He is endowed with twelve arms, adorned with serpents, bones, and jewels;
he is wrathful, possesses a half-liṅga, and is filled with the splendor of the cremation ground.
One should fashion him with a garment made of six [skins], and by that means,
he wears a tiger-skin mantle, is adorned with a garland of skulls,
utters the sound "Hūṃ Hūṃ," and brandishes a great sword.
Holding in his hands a trident, sword, discus, bell, goad, and the gesture of granting boons;
[and] holding a threatening gesture, aśoka flower, mace, bow, noose, the gesture of fearlessness, and a small bell.
Having displayed the mudrās beginning with the invocation (āvāhana) and having performed worship,
the practitioner should then meditate upon Mārtaṇḍa Bhairava, whose limbs begin with the syllable *hrām*.
Then, having offered a handful of flowers along with the *arghya* and the mantra:
*Hrauṃ Hsauṃḥ Kulamārtaṇḍabhairavāya Śrīṃ Hrauṃ 5 Śrī*.
Afterwards, having sprinkled himself with water, he should again recite this leaf;
then he should properly cast a handful of flowers toward Savitṛ, the witness of all actions.
5 *sauṃḥ* *kṣrīṃ* *kṣyauṃ* *hsauṃḥ* *phaṭ* *kṣiphreṃ* *māṃ* *sphuṭa* *hmrauṃ* *kṣyauṃ* *sau* *śrī*. This is the mantra for the handful of flowers (*puṣpāñjali*).
As for the mudrā, it consists of the trident and the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*) performed three times by me, the devourer of the sacrifice (*kāhāriṇī*).
Then, having displayed the half-finger mudrā, [one should place it] upon the eight petals starting from the east.
In the center, one should worship Caṇḍaroṣaṇī, who holds a trident and the gesture of threatening (tarjanī);
one should join her with the nine Śaktis and worship the Bhairavas as well.

Salutation everywhere to Khecarīmudrā. Having performed the visualization of the limbs of dissolution (layāṅga), the limbs of enjoyment (bhogāṅga), and the ritual procedures beginning with *hrām*, one should worship with dūrvā grass and red flowers, along with incense, lamps, and food offerings (*naivedya*), accompanied by mantras.
Having recited [the mantra] as much as possible, one should offer the *arghya* with the *arghya-mantra*;
and one should place the previously mentioned *arghya-mantra* within the heart-lotus of the Sun.
One should extract both the small ether (daharākāśa) and the supreme self (kūtastha);
having offered the arghya water to the Lord, one should finally perform the oblation into the fire.
Having drawn a four-cornered mandala with the syllable *Iṃ* on the left side,
one should place a beautiful vessel containing its support upon it.
The preceptor, having worshipped Paśumārtaṇḍa and its mantra:
5 hrāṃ hrīṃ saḥ paśumārtaṇḍa bhairavāya namaḥ 5 śrī.
One should offer the remnants of the worship and the floral remains to everyone. Thus ends the Saura-pūjā.
7a) Furthermore, the worship of the *caru-maṇḍala* is not prescribed here;
for it is established that [the practice] belongs to the past and so forth, being based on that [earlier] tradition.
In the midst of the gurus of the supreme reality is the circle of gurus, Bhairava;
beginning with the Śāmbhavī worship, it is unstained by the central *saṃkā*.
Having emerged from that [place], he performed the necessary purifications at the conclusion of his solar worship for the sake of the Great-Souled One who possesses all auspicious qualities.
Then that practitioner, Ucchaka, who was the lord of the six lineages,
completed the Śrīpūrṇamandira [temple], which possessed the remainder of the Sāman chants.
Entering daily with the breath, preceded by the word *pada*, using the *unmaṇi-mudrā*,
[one should worship] one's own Lord Gaṇapati, as well as Durgā and Sarasvatī.
One should assign the three fields— the supreme self along with its respective seeds—
to the head, the right shoulder, the left shoulder, the two thighs, and the heart.
Having worshipped [the deity] with lotus bark and other offerings,
and having understood the established rule of the scriptures that this is the supreme [practice], one should then enter the pavilion.
Facing either the northeast or whichever direction is appropriate,
seated upon a throne, one should worship Ādibhairava.
Śrī Śambhu does not disregard the pair of feet of the high-souled worshipper; therefore, one should never show disrespect toward him, for he is the source of all things.
He consecrated the glorious ones.
Facing the northeast (Īśāna), and likewise not facing the opposite direction,
one should worship Śambhu according to one's discernment, together with the sixfold Śakti.
And according to this direction for the worship of these deities,
a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) bestowed in such a manner bestows immortality.
The knower of mantras should prepare the seat with this mantra;
for one devoid of the mantra-seat has no authority for the worship of Śiva.
Then, from that heart, [the mantra] ending with "bhagavatyante" [is recited], followed by "nīlavajrāsane," then "mama jīvarakṣa yugaṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā," and finally "kāma."
7b) 5 Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One who sits upon the blue vajra-throne; protect my life, protect it! Hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!
Having thus sat upon the mantra-seat according to the ritual procedure, the practitioner [should proceed].
One should contemplate the hands as Śiva and Śakti, located on the right and left respectively;
through that, one should attain a state of union and then perform three rhythmic claps (tāla).
Thereafter, one should fashion the binding of the directions with fire arising from that very [mantra],
performing the circumambulation three times starting from the east and northeast, and extending from the head down to the feet.
Having uttered the five *praṇavas*, one should bring the five elements to dissolution.
In due order, [one attains] the Lord who is the soul of all, the power of the root-instruction, whose nature is Śiva.
In the state of union with the Yonimudrā, one should again raise Kuṇḍalinī from the root and join her with the mantra "Mhīṃ," which is the seed-syllable of Śakti.
In the Mūlādhāra, at the tip of the penis, there is a full lotus;
in the Svādhiṣṭhāna, one should reside on the letter Va, surrounded by the letters beginning with Va and ending with La.
The sixteen-petaled [lotus] consists of the Kaṭha-sounds and the vowels;
the two-petaled [lotus] of the Viśuddhi and Ājñā [cakras] consists of the letters Ha and Kṣa, respectively.
The triad of disgust alone exists in its distinct forms within the auspicious state;
in that supreme, full bliss of consciousness, it takes the form of the threefold refuge.
Having joined [the breaths], dry out the body preceded by the practice of breath-extension (pavanāyāma);
O Śivā, having performed both contraction and expansion, remain constantly for a moment.
But with the mental fluctuations dissolved in reverse order,
one reaches the imperishable state, endowed with primordial power (ādi-śakti) and situated upon the six gods.
Having dissolved the body into the state of Śambhu, one should again unite one's own self [with it].
This is its meaning:
having firmly bound the Yonimudrā, one should then [raise] Kuṇḍalinī from the root (mūla).

Having slowly raised [the disciple] with the syllable *sphauṃ* by means of the *akula-ātman*, and having united him with Śiva, one should utter *hrīṃ* for him. By the mind alone, from the unstruck (*ahanāhata*) state, one should [unite him] with the wind by means of the *yonimudrā*.
Or, together with the power of whichever root [mantra], one should well join it;
for by the restraint of breath (prāṇasaṃyama), the union of the Kula and Akula occurs in this very manner.
He who performs this is indeed a yogi, he is liberated, and he is a Kaulika;
for he has restrained his vital breath by means of the six accumulations and the great jewels.
In this very manner, one should subsequently perform the network of ritual placements (nyāsajāla) three times;
one should carry out the network of placements according to the scriptures and in the proper sequence.
Having uttered the five *praṇavas*, one should thereafter recite the mantra;
then, the *praṇava* in reverse order—this is the definitive rule for the weapon-mantra (*śāstrāstra*).
And so it is said:
The three-eyed Śrīmāsa has proclaimed these essence-mantras (sattimantras),
which are arranged in both direct (anuloma) and reverse (viloma) order, with the syllable *yaṃ* situated between them and the *praṇava*.
And thus it is said.
Having prostrated before the glorious Guru, Gaṇanātha, Vāgīśa, and likewise Vaṭuka, I shall declare this supreme compendium of the essence of mantras.
In all instances, such as in worship and other rites, one should employ the sequential placement (kramānyāsa);
having performed the nyāsa of the five jewels (pañcaratna) upon the fingers beginning with the little finger.
Then one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) of the root-vidyā and the three-limbed placement (tryaṅganyāsa);
thereafter, one should perform the seed-syllable placement (bījanyāsa), followed immediately by the jewel placement (ratnanyāsa).

After performing the threefold nyāsa beginning with the supreme (parā), one should subsequently practice meditation; the placement of the limb-mantras is prescribed upon the fingers, starting from the little finger, in their proper order.
Having also performed the placement of the hands (karanyāsa) upon the two palms,
the placement (nyāsa) in the locations beginning with the heart was then joyfully and respectfully performed.
Likewise, [one should place] the Cācāra-form on the left, and the Śruti-mukha-śuci on the right;
then one should perform the Vaktra-nyāsa upon one's own head, consisting of twelve syllables.
The preceptor, being equanimous, should perform the installation of Ājñā, Viśuddhi, Hṛt, and Nābhi in the Svādhiṣṭhāna and other centers,
as previously described, having performed the supreme and other nyāsas.
Likewise, having placed the Tārās and the jewels upon the fingers beginning with the little finger, one performs the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) with the root mantra.

Now, meditation.
Resplendent like a thousand suns, the glorious one, the supreme Śambhu— eternal and imperishable— moves about, bearing great light and weight, with six faces.
His eyes flash from the six sense-bases; he is adorned with eighteen ornaments and decorated with a tiger-skin loincloth and a garland of severed heads.
Upon the firm jewel-tree of men, he is completely enveloped by garlands of flowers;
his supreme [form] is held by the Brahma-navel, the thumb, the tusks, and the staff.
Adorned with various ornaments, he who has removed the bonds of all beings from every side,
possesses a great body and holds a trident, a spear, a javelin, and a horn as his excellent weapons.
Mata is depicted holding a skull, a fruit, a bow, a noose, and displaying the gesture of fearlessness;
she sports in the Devāvṛta cremation ground, her mind and heart fixed on the Mānasottara mountain.
Thus one should meditate upon the Supreme Goddess as being covered by breasts and the source [of generation];
having realized the mental Śābhava state, one should recite the Vidyā with undistracted mind.
Having meditated thus and recited these [mantras], one should again recite the two root-vidyās;
having performed the special worship, the two feet are consecrated with the arghya water.
The lineage of gurus is upon the head.

one should place upon that a vessel with its base, which is purified by mantra.
Having established [the vessel] and filled it with milk, as well as the waters in the supporting vessels,
one should worship the Vahnikalā in the center, together with the letters beginning with 'ya' in the support (ādhāra).

16a) *Oṃ* *raṃ*, obeisance to the seat of the general *arghya* vessel, which is the fire-mandala, possesses smoky flames, and consists of ten kalās. Then, having washed and established the vessel, one should worship the gems within it.

Furthermore, one should worship the twelve *kalās* in the middle of the vessel, conjoined with the letters from *ka* to *bha*. *Haṃ sūryamaṇḍalāya tapinyādi-dvādaśa-kalātmane sāmānyārghya-pātrāya namaḥ.* (Salutation to the general offering vessel, which is the solar orb consisting of the twelve *kalās* beginning with *Tapinī*.)
Having filled [the vessel] with pure water, or with water mixed with the causal substances,
one who is restrained in speech should worship the sixteen vowels together with the sixteen digits (kalās).

5. Having offered this general arghya (oblation) to the Moon-maṇḍala— the essence of the sixteen digits beginning with nectar— saying "Obeisance to the nectar of the general arghya," and having established the Kula in the center,
one should likewise consecrate it with the mantras, and furthermore with the supreme Śrīvidyā.
One should [perform this] seven times or three times with the vidyā of Paraśambhu.

Having worshipped with the Śrīvidyā in three parts, having worshipped with the *pareśvara* seed-syllable three or seven times, having honored it with perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and having displayed the *dhenu-mudrā*—
this is the procedure for the general *arghya*. Having established the peaceful [deity] to its right, thereafter...
Having performed the ritual sprinkling with the five substances beginning with *vakṣaṇī*, one should recite the *Ghaṭasūtra*.
One should recite the passage beginning with "The ocean being churned" (*samudramathyamānābhyādi*). One should worship as in the case of the general *arghya* offering;
having poured that drop into the general *arghya*, and having joined oneself with the materials for worship, one performs the drawing of the mandala.
One should perform [it].
The square, the half-moon, the triangle, the hexagon, the tree,
again the triangle, the crescent moon, and the ninefold nature consisting of the Nāda and Bindu.
O Śrī Bhairava, wherever there may be space for the special arghya-maṇḍalas, one should properly draw this Navātman [maṇḍala] accordingly.
16b) Then,

for the purpose of worship according to the Śāmbhava Āgama, one should draw the upper mandala; therein, starting from the east and ending in the center at the upper region, according to the instruction of the Guru.
One should recite the six seed-syllables in sequence, joined with the *praṇava* (OM) at the beginning and end: *laṃ vaṃ raṃ yaṃ haṃ saṃ*, and so forth.
O God, it may indeed be square, half-moon, triangular, hexagonal, or circular.
Having uttered the five *praṇavas*, one should then write [the syllables] within three circles.

Then that wise one, the venerable Bhairava, stood beneath the crop of grain for the sake of the essential meaning; having knelt with his knees upon the ground, he remained at a height of sixteen finger-breadths.
Having drawn a square measuring either twenty-four finger-breadths or twelve finger-breadths, and having fashioned a lotus in its center;
One should draw a lotus with eight petals using silver and gold; within that, one should place three mandalas arranged in a circular form.
One should write with camphor, sandalwood, and the like, as well as musk and saffron; using a mixture of lac, resin, and beeswax, one should inscribe it upon a golden plate or similar surface.
One should properly draw an excellent white lotus with eight petals naturally radiant, possessing a pericarp of supreme nature, together with the sun and gold.
Let there be garments such as silk scarves spread upon the ground;
however, they should be placed below the lotus, to the left of the ordinary *arghya* vessel.
The wise one should draw the special *arghya*-maṇḍala like the general one;

on both sides of the lotus, at its two northern faces, he should draw two maṇḍalas measuring four finger-breadths, extending eastward. [He should also draw those] for the three door-keepers and the preceptors.
One should arrange the fivefold sequence in the northeast and the three and five locations in the south;
one should place the door-protectors in the north and the mandalas of the powerful ones.
Then, with flowers, unbroken rice grains, and one's own arghya offerings, one performs the worship of the special arghya.
Having made the vessel common [to all], and having performed the rites up to its placement,
one should worship it with the *nidāna* together with a companion, as before.
Having invoked the Kuṇḍalī-mudrā, which holds the sacrificial pit filled with unbroken rice grains,
one should [visualize] Kuṇḍalinī rising from the root, possessing a radiance equal to ten million moons.
Having pierced the mandala of the six chakras, the Suṣumṇā, pervading the void,
pierces the plane of the Moon and Sun and comes to rest in the state of Śambhu.
Having meditated upon the one endowed with splendor, [the syllables] white and red, mixed together,
emerge from the two nostrils produced by the three feet.
Having filled the special *arghya* vessel and consecrated it with glances that render it nectar-like,
one should meditate upon it as resembling a blazing fire and display the *dhenu-mudrā*.
O you who have arisen from a fragment of the cosmic egg, cause this path to flash forth within my mind; svāhā! svāhā! svāhā!

Having thus prayed, one should also worship with the following mantras: 5 Hsrauḥ | Huḥ Amṛteśodbhavāya Huḥ Hsrauḥ 5 Śrī | 5 Aiṃ Parāmṛtavettanyam Aiṃ 5 Śrī | 5 Oṃ Juṃ Saḥ Amṛteśa Bhairavāya Saḥ Juṃ Oṃ Amṛta Śrī Bhairavyai Oṃ Juṃ Saḥ ||
5 Śrī.
Having consecrated [the substances] with the two vidyās, one should touch [them] with the ring finger;
having uttered the Navātma and the Kūṭa, [one should also touch them] while joined with the Navātmikā.
Then, one should again worship that arghya with those drops three times;
one should consecrate the limbs and so forth, as well as the deity and the ritual resolve (saṃkalpa), with the root mantra.
This specific *arghya* has been shown according to the instruction of one’s own guru.

Having performed the sprinkling as before, one should perform the purification of the elements (*bhūta-viśodhana*). *Hasakṣamalavarayūṃ sahakṣamalavarayīrī oṃ surādevyai arghyam ārīśvaryai vauṣaṭ.* *Sahakṣamalavarayaṃ.*
Ī HASA KṢA MALA VARA YAYŪ & AṂ SAḤ ṢAḤ. OṂ Ānandabhairava-Ānandanātha Navātmaka Parāmbā Śrī.

Having displayed the seven mudrās beginning with invocation (āvāhana), one should contemplate the vowels of the sixteen [groups] within the triangle in the middle of the vessel starting from 'A' and so forth— namely Aṃ 15, Ka 15, Thaṃ 15— with Haṃ as the hundred-thousandth in the center. Then, one should worship the four seats (pīṭhas) in the corners with their respective mantras.
Having extracted the sixteen-fold Root Vidyā (Mūlavidyā) which is eternal, and having extracted the mantra taught by the Guru of Śrīvidyā—
having recited three times: "Amṛte amṛtodbhave amṛtavarṣiṇī amṛtavarṣaya 2 śrāṃ śrīṃ śruṃ amṛteśvaraṃ amṛteśvarye namaḥ"— [this is] for Ānandabhairava.

*vauṣaṭ*. Six [syllables] to Ānandabhairavī. Thus, having performed the *saṃmohana* (the rite of enchantment), then follows the lineage of the Gurus (*gurukrama*). The mantra of the Lord of the Seven Principles (*tatvareśvara*) together with Asitāṅga is recited seven times. Having projected the portions (*aṃśāni*) upon the God and Goddess, one should fashion the six limbs (*ṣāṅga*) with the protection mantra. The *vidyā* of Saubhāgya consists of the *vidyās* of Śrī, Putrī, and so forth. 5 *haṃsaḥ so'haṃ*. *oṃ*.

Phāṃ Phīṃ Sau Aṃ Niśānānandanatha Haṃra Cāmupakrāśānandanā Śrī. Likewise, [offer] the seven ancillaries (sapta-upacāra). Thus is the procedure for purification (pūti-vidhi). Having meditated upon the identity (*tādātmya*) with the special offering water (*viśeṣārghya*), having arranged the five offerings (*pañcopacāra*), [place] the special [offering] in the square mandala on the right, in a vessel of nāga-pattern. Aiṃ. Thus.

Having established [the vessel] with *klīṃ*, having poured [the liquid] with the first [syllable] *mauḥ* and so forth, and having consecrated it with special water; having worshipped with the *arghya* water using the solar [mantra] and having specially consecrated it, one should remember the feet of one’s own Guru for the purification of sacrifice and giving. In the center is the venerable Guru-Nātha, ending with the supreme word (*paropadānta*), and upon the head is the lineage of Gurus (*gurukrama*).
One should perform worship; having offered the five-fold services (pañcopacāra), one should cast the remainder into the fire of one's own self.
18a) The knower of mantras, O Lord, should restrain the deity who is the very essence of the mantra, abiding in the form of an internal visualization within his own body.
Having fully adorned oneself with fragrant tilakas and various ornaments according to the extent of one's means, [one should proceed].
One should worship the Āgama-maṇḍala with the mantras to be mentioned hereafter;
and while exhaling through the right nostril, one should perform the worship with the Praṇavas.

5 Aiṃ, obeisance to the twenty-eight *krama* mandalas. 5 Hsauṃ, to the great preta lotus-seat, hsrau 5 Śrī 5 Aiṃ, to the foot pervading the *praṇava* mandala, Vicce Aiṃ 5, obeisance. With these [mantras], one should worship with flowers and unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and with the *arghya* water drops; having established [the deity] there in the mandala.

One should worship in the Śāmbhava maṇḍala. According to the instruction of the Guru, [the deities] are in the south, north, east, west, and in the middle. The mantra-deities are to be addressed with the *tāra* (oṃ) enclosed by *tāra*s:
*aiṃ* to the mantra-deity *aiṃ* five times;
*hrīṃ* to the mantra-deity *hrīṃ* five times; *śrīṃ* to the mantra-deity *śrīṃ* five times; *hphreṃ* to the mantra-deity.
Hphreṃ 5 | 5 Hsauḥ; for the mantra deity, Hsau 5.
One should worship the two goddesses together in the center upon a lotus seat through a single yoga.
Having performed the rites beginning with the invocation (āvāhana), one should display the mudrās and specifically the yoni-mudrā.
One should offer incense, lamps, and food offerings while reciting the mantra prescribed for that;
having thus worshipped the single Āgama, one should then [proceed] upon the eight-petaled lotus.
One should worship the three mandalas in the surrounding area and in the center with the mantras to be mentioned hereafter, according to the prescribed method.

5 vaṃ, obeisance to the moon-maṇḍala, vaṃ 5 śrī; 5 haṃ, obeisance to the sun-maṇḍala, haṃ 5; 5 raṃ, obeisance to the fire-maṇḍala; obeisance to the twenty-eight maṇḍalas, śrī; 5 hsau, obeisance to the great preta lotus-seat, hsau 5.
Having established a well-characterized Śiva-liṅga in the center of the lotus, one should place it there with arghya,
flowers, and akṣata, facing north with its head toward the west.
18b) Likewise, I worship Vahnipreta with Svāhā and the gods with "me" (five times). Hrīṃ Jātavedase Hrīṃ (five times);
Oṃ Hrīṃ Svāhāyai Hrīṃ Oṃ (five times). Having meditated upon the two [deities] holding excellent power-shafts, [one should place them] at their navel and on the head.
Having meditated upon the syllable *ekāra* as the supreme meditation, one should worship it as *aiṃkāra*.
Then, having invoked the God and Goddess into the midst of that, one should worship them.
Having meditated upon the mudrās for invocation and so forth, and having performed the ritual of the limbs (aṅganyāsa),
one should offer the services of worship with perfumes, flowers, unbroken rice grains, and other offerings.
One should worship the Eight Auspicious Ones (*aṣṭamaṅgala*) on the lotus petals starting from the east:
Aiṃ 5 Hūṃ Maṅgala Mahābhairavānandanātha Hrāṃ Hrīṃ Brahmāṇī Devyambā Hrīṃ 5 Śrī. 5 Sūṃ Carcika Mahābhairavānandanātha Sūṃ Śrīṃ Māheśvarī.

Devyaṃvā Śrī 5 | 5 Kṣuṃ Yoga Mahābhairavānandanātha Kṣaṃ Kṣī Kaumārī Devyaṃvā Kṣīṃ 5 | 5 Mūṃ Harasiddha Mahābhairavānandanātha Mūṃ Śrīṃ Vaiṣṇavī Devyaṃvā Mīṃ 5 | Lūṃ Bhaṭṭa Mahābhairavānandanātha Lūṃ Līṃ Vārāhī.
Devī Ambā Līṃ 5 Śrī 5 Kūṃ Kili 2 Mahābhairavānandanātha Vūṃ Vī Indrāṇī Devī Ambā Vīṃ 5.
5 YŪṂ Kālarātri Mahābhairavānandanātha, YŪṂ YĪṂ Cāmuṇḍā Devyambā, YĪṂ 5. 5 RUṂ Bhīṣaṇa Mahābhairavānandanātha, RUṂ RĪṂ Kamalā DevyavārīṂ 5.
Now, meditation.
The Cuvukas and the Rājahastas, as well as the goddesses of graceful form,
and the goddesses holding skull-bowls and tridents, resemble the rising sun.
They are red in color and possess three eyes, adorned with all ornaments;
all are sixteen years of age and have intensely rolling eyes.
Having separated the eight seed-syllables and joined them with the ninth,
one should worship that liquor of the Veśa-kūṭa together with the anusvāra.
One should worship with peak mantras (kūṭamantra) joined with secret powers (guhyaśakti) and with hymns;
thereafter, one should worship the lineage of gurus (gurukrama) according to the sequence of the tradition (saṃpradāya).
19a) One should worship the five gurus: Ādinātha, Anādinātha, Kulaguru, as well as those known as Acintya and Mitra.
Of these five, four possess powers whose nature is grace;
they move through the regions below, above, and in the middle, according to their sequence.
For example:
5 ĀṂ Ādigurunātha Ādyāmbā ĀṂ 5 Śrī 5 AṂ Anādigurunātha Anāmbā AṂ 5.
Kuṃkuleśvarānandanātha, Kulesvaryā, or Kuṃ 5 Śrī0. Aṃ Anādigurunātha, Acintyāmbā, Aṃ 5. Miṃ Mitragurunātha, Mitrīmbā, Miṃ 5.
Having addressed the five Gurus as endowed with the five powers,
one should offer the ritual services, beginning with water for the feet, preceded by the Praṇava.
Then, after the sequence of the gurus, one should worship the two deities on all sides;
the Goddess and the venerable Guru-deity are established according to their respective seats (*pīṭha*).
Having again worshipped the goddesses in the limbs of dissolution, such as the heart and so forth,
one should worship the six limbs in the directions of fire, the northeast, the southwest, and the northwest.
In the corners, in the center, and in the cardinal directions,
one should sequentially arrange the limbs of enjoyment— namely incense and so forth— with the heart mantra.
One should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to one's ability with a focused mind on the two *vidyās*.

Having bowed and offered praise, one should then laud [the deities] with the five verses beginning with "Homage to the one who possesses the *uḍḍīna* lotus" (*namo uḍḍīnavaktra*). Then, one should worship the three mandalas as previously described.
Resembling a pool of moonlight, it rests upon the back of Śaśā.

One should worship the three-eyed one who has come for the sake of favoring the practitioner, who holds a trident and a half-threatening finger (tarjanī), and whose hands are adorned with ornaments in sequence.
Hmauṃ to Niśāṭanātha, Hyauṃ 5 Śrī.
In the mandala, one should worship the Sun in the east, possessing the previously described characteristics of battle; seated upon the back of a horse, his body is of yellow complexion.

5 HRAUṂ TAMĀLAYE HRĪṂ 5. In the center of the mandala, one should worship the Fire-god, who possesses the previously described weapons and characteristics, who resembles powdered saffron, and who is mounted upon a ram.
19b) KṢAUṂ KĀLĀNALĀYA KṢAUṂ 5.
One should worship the six supreme [deities] beginning with Śrīnātha and ending with Paryanta in their proper sequence.
Then, for the destruction of obstacles, [one should place] Heramba and Vaśya to the left.
One should invoke the mandala situated within the heart into the square [mandala],
having performed the six-limbed rite with "llām" and so forth.
Meditate!
White in complexion, holding an elephant, a horse, an axe, a half-toothed trident,
and a staff in his four arms, he is seated upon a rat.
One should recite "Lakṣaika-vighna-saṃghāta-haraṃ tītaṃ śajaṃvaca glauṃ herambāya glauṃ" five times.
Then, one should meditate upon the Supreme Lord and offer the primary mantra.
Then follows the lineage of the gurus.
Furthermore, having placed the vessel upon its support— a triangular mandala situated beneath the Heramba mandala— filled with wine and joined with a drop (bindu).
One should perform the five services with the five *praṇavas*.

Having placed the common vessel upon the triangular mandala and worshipped it with the five *praṇavas* using perfumes, flowers, and unbroken rice grains; [one offers] the water-oblation (*vali*) full to the brim, accompanied by the first and second [mantras],
ending with *hrīṃ sarvavighnakṛdbhyaḥ sarvabhūtebhyaḥ*.
HŪṂ PHAṬ SVĀHĀ. With this sacrificial formula (yaktyākāra), one should offer the bali. Having displayed the khecarī-mudrā and the yoni-mudrā, one carries out the command (ājñā-puraścaraṇa).
One should display the bowl, surrounded by the Bhūtas, with the index finger.
5. Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ! Having drawn her mantra from the heart, one should cast the offering (bali).

Then, having sprinkled the water for the *argha* offering or the external [elements], one should perform an oblation (*homa*) for their gratification. One should mentally effect the unification of the *liṅga*, the limbs, and one's own self as desired. Furthermore, on the head, one should worship the lineage of gurus (*gurukrama*), and then, with devotion, one should worship the *kaṇṭha* (throat); thus, one becomes identical with the *śāmbhava* [state].
Having thoroughly worshipped the Great Lord, the Master of the Great Cremation Ground.
20a) One should meditate upon the ninefold self in the form of a hexagonal mandala within the pericarp of a lotus,
together with millions of sages, lords of yogis, yoginīs, Bhairavas, and others.
Being served by Mahāśambhu, he faces all directions in every way.
Having worshipped the great cremation ground, immediately thereafter the kṣatrapīṭha,
and having worshipped the trees and creepers, as well as the nooses within the maṇḍala.
Then one should reverently worship the trees beginning with the *śirīṣa*, the deities beginning with Caṇḍa, Bhairava,
and likewise the serpents beginning with Ananta, starting from the east and ending in the northeast.

Having thus properly worshipped the eight [deities] who bear swords and shields, who are endowed with knowledge, and whose forms are like the moon, and having performed the rite for the protection of the kṣatriyas;
Having meditated upon the deities residing within one's own body, one should offer the oblation;
and with the three [mantras] beginning with Triśāttana, one should offer it to the guardians at the gateway pavilion.
In the pure field known as Prayoga, joined by Sudṛś and Yoginīmatī,
situated in the supreme and inferior great pīṭha, O Śrī Navātmikā!
One should thus worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, unbroken grains (akṣata), and other offerings.
That is to say:

5. Homage to the Great Cremation Ground (Mahāśmaśāna). || 5 || 25. To the sacred field of Prayāga. 25. To the Kalpa-tree. 5. To the radiant Jyotiṣmatī creeper. 5. To the guardians of the Great Cremation Ground. 5. One should perform the worship of the Polaka. 5. Homage to the Śirīṣa tree. 5. To the Karañja tree. 5. To the Aśvattha tree. 5. To the Dāḍima tree. 5. To the Bilva tree. 5. [To the Bilva tree. || 5 ||
To Raktaśauka, 5 | 5; to Cyūta, 5 | 5; to Vaḍha, 5 | 5; to Caṇḍabhairava, 5 | 5; to Krodhabhairava, 5 | 5;
to Gaṃ Gahvarabhairava, 5; to Jvālāmālākulabhairava, 5; to Bhīṣaṇabhairava, 5; to Ghorāndhakārabhairava, 5 | 5; to Lakṣmīdharabhairava, 5 | 5; to Karāla...
To Bhairava, five, five; to Ananta, five, five; to Vāsuki, five, five; to Takṣaka, five, five; to Karkoṭhaka, five, five; to Śaṅkha, five, [20b] five.
Worship [the deities] in clockwise order starting from the east: five times for Mahāśaṅkha, five times for Padma, and five times for Mahāpadma.
Now, meditation.
[He saw] a terrifying banner with a burning human limb, resting upon the shoulder of a bull,
topped with a trident, a hand-axe, and a severed head, and holding a blood-stained skull-cup.
Bearing their lotus-faces cast down as they were threatened by the Great King,
they stood with one foot lingering behind, guarding the great cremation ground.
Yellow, red, blue, white, green, black, crimson, and pure white— each of these eight [colors] has the face of a lion, a tiger, Śiva, a horse, a boar, a monkey, a bull, and a swan respectively.
And [he saw] terrifying beings with faces like bears, bulls,
crocodiles, and lions, as well as serpents wearing skins and human beings of supreme form.
Having thus worshipped them perfectly and performed the rite for protection against injury,
one should offer the final oblation while contemplating these very [deities] as residing within one's own body.
Then one should worship the Tiraskaraṇī (the Veil). After that, the lineage of gurus (gurukrama).

5 *Hklīṃ* to the two thumbs (*aṅguṣṭha*), *namaḥ*. 5 *Bhagavatī* to the two index fingers (*tarjanī*), *namaḥ*. 5 *Māheśvarī* to the two middle fingers (*madhyamā*). 5 *Sarvajana-cakṣus-tiraskaraṇaṃ* to the two ring fingers (*anāmikā*). 5 *Kuru kuru* to the two little fingers (*kaniṣṭhikā*).
5 *Svāhā* to the palms and backs of the hands (*karatala-pṛṣṭha*). In this same manner, [apply to] the heart and other limbs.
Having arranged the pervasive [deity], one should meditate.
One should contemplate the group of animals as having disheveled hair, their bodies naked yet adorned with all ornaments, and as being distressed from the sight of their own female organs.

Then, the devotee should meditate upon her who dwells within the triangle situated in the center of the heart-lotus, who is the destroyer of obstacles and whose nature is the protection of her devotees; she is dark-complexioned, slightly trembling, endowed with three red eyes,
and holds a mace and a sword in her two hands.
And with her two enchanting arms, Khajūrī holds a water-pot.
Mounted upon a blue horse, wandering about, clad in blue garments, ornaments, garlands,
and ointments, O Blessed One, bearing a sword as your weapon, may you protect your devotees by bringing the worlds to sleep with the sound of your footfall.

Having mentally prepared the fivefold offerings, one should indeed accept the worship with causes such as flowers, unbroken rice grains (*akṣata*), and so forth; then, having performed protection, [one recites]: *Hm klīm namo bhagavati māheśvari sarvavaśīkaraṇacakṣustiraskaraṇīṃ kuru 2 svāhā*. Thus is the rite of invisibility (*tiraskaraṇa*). Again, on the head is the lineage of the Gurus.
The mental, the ethereal, the aerial, the fiery,
the watery, and the earthly— these six are the auspicious powers of the Sovereign.
O Kuleśānī, the wise one should meditate upon [the deity] within the hexagon at the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra);
likewise, one should worship Mānasa in the northeastern corner of that hexagon.
The Nābhasa [element] is in the eastern corner, likewise Āgneya and Māruta;
Tejas is declared to be in the south-west, and Apas in the west.
O Goddess, the wise one should worship the earthly [element] for Vāyu in due order;
O Ocean of Nectar, [this consists of] the sixfold collection beginning with the mental [space] and ending with earth.
One should contemplate the four Marīcis, each possessing four syllables.
Thus ends the manual for mental worship.
Salutations to the venerable Guru Śambhu. Now begins the worship of Vicceśvara.
The seed-syllable (kūṭa) of Vicceśvara is like crystal in the Viśuddhi-cakra;
one should meditate upon the Lord, born from that, as one's own self within the heart.

5 HMRĀṂ PHRĀṂ to the two thumbs; HRĪṂ PHRĪṂ to the two index fingers; 5 HPHRAIṂ PHRAIṂ to the two middle fingers; 5 HMAUṂ PHRAUṂ to the two ring fingers; 5 HPHRAṂḤ PHREṂḤ to the palms and backs of the hands. In this manner, one should perform the placement (nyāsa) on the heart and other limbs.
Now, meditation.
Resembling pure crystal, possessing six faces and twelve arms, he has the splendor of Bhairava; he holds a trident, a discus, a noose of kuśa grass, and arrows in his hands.
In her left [hands], she holds the threatening gesture (*tarjanī*), the conch, and the banner;
likewise, she bears the bow and the gesture of fearlessness (*abhaya*) as Kuleśvarī.
Having meditated thus upon Devakūṭa with [the mantra] joined by long vowels,
one should perform the three-limbed rite for these [deities] in sequence, enclosed by the Praṇavas.
And the Goddess, possessing a divine luster, stands upon his body by virtue of his power,
holding a sword, a trident, an upward-pointing arrow, a bow, a noose, a goad, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Holding a book, a spear, and a half-moon, she wears universal earrings.
Having meditated in this manner according to the path stated in the root text, one should then install that [deity] once more.
Having meditated thus.

[He saw] a mantra of ten syllables, resembling split black collyrium,

Appearing about sixteen years of age, his bones were coated with jewels and gold;

With his face like that of a lion,

The door of Alābhṛvardhaka is adorned with a hip-belt and lotuses;

The *pārijāta* tree, a rosary for recitation, a book, and the gesture of granting fearlessness are his favorites;
moreover, with his two remaining arms, he tears apart the skin of Brahmā.

The form known as the Samaya is said to be more essential than those;

Having recollected her— whether she has ten faces or six faces— as the peaceful one who brings satisfaction,

she who is adorned with the goad, the noose, the discus, the conch, the mace, and the jewel.

The seer (ṛṣi) of this Śrīnamonta-Śivamālā-mantra is Bhagindrāditya; the meter (chandaḥ) is Jagatī; the deity (devatā) is the Great Bhaṭṭārika named Sarvajña, who dwells at the seat (pīṭha) of the Bhaṭṭāraka [beginning with] the syllable *sa*—the King of Enjoyment (*bhogayara*)—who is the beloved of Sarasvatī, the one adorned with a charming lap, the all-knowing, and the one whose movement is according to desire; [this is for] the accomplishment of iron (*lohasiddhi*).
The application [of this mantra] is as follows: O Śivā, by the touch of the hand of your devotee, the eightfold types of iron are [transformed].
It attains a golden state, through which it becomes equal to Śiva.
Oṃ, salutation to Tripurasundarī; salutation, etc. || 7 ||

Of this Śrī-Svāhānta-Śivamālā-mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) is Vivasvat Āditya, the presiding deity of the sense of sight; the meter (chandaḥ) is Atijagatī; the seat (pīṭha) is situated at the letter *ka* belonging to the King of Desire (*kāmarāja*). The deity is the venerable Lord Kāmeśvara, named Kāmamada, whose lap is adorned by Kamalā and Amalalalitā, [accompanied] by the eight [siddhis] beginning with Aṇimā.
The application is in the accomplishment [of the goal].
In those [beings], qualities such as atomization (aṇimā) and magnification (mahimā), manifested according to one's own will through the body,
are known as the powers (guṇas) belonging to the masters of the bodies of Your devotees. (4)
Oṃ, salutation to Tripurasundarī, svāhā, and so forth. || 8 ||

Of this Śivamālā mantra, ending with *śrītarpamī*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Puruṣāditya, the presiding deity of the sense of touch; the meter (*chandaḥ*) is Śakvarī; and its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of total subjugation through the mango tree associated with the Lord of Liberation (*mokṣedārāja*).
Having offered their bodies, wealth, and lives like your own servants, they serve you as your devotees; thus, O King, the women have become your attendants.
Oṃ, salutations to Tripurasundara; I offer libations, salutations, and so forth. || 9 ||
Of this *Śrījayajayānta-śivamālā-mantra*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is the Sun, who presides over the sense of hearing.

The deity (*devatā*) is the Lord Kāmeśvara, who resides upon the seat (*pīṭha*) of the Lord Muktidara-rājasa-lekharabhaṭṭāraka, adorned with the name Lakṣmī and graced by the tongue named Kolatā. Its application (*viniyoga*) is for the purpose of universal attraction (*sarvākarṣaṇa*).
Those who are well-restrained by iron shackles and fetters indeed fall into the hands of those devoted to you, who draw them out like iron from ore.
Oṃ, salutations! Victory, victory, O Tripurasundarī! And so forth. || 10 ||
Of this glorious Śuddha-Śivamālā-mantra, the seer (ṛṣi) is the Sun with consciousness, presiding over the principle of ego (ahaṃkāra-tattva);

the meter (chandas) is the Yoṣṭi; the deity (devatā) is the Lord Ekāmeśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, who resides at the seat of the venerable Lord Hrīṃkāra, is adorned by Hiraṇyadāna Lalitā, and is the enchantment of all.
The application [of the mantra] is for the sake of attaining success.
O Ambikā, by the mere glance of you upon your devotees, [all their desires are fulfilled].
"What should be done by you who are bewildered? Men, women, kings, and others should offer [this]:
'Oṃ namaḥ tripurasundari', 'Oṃ namas tripurasundare', and so forth. (11)

For this [mantra] Śrīnamontamithunamālāmūrti, the seer (ṛṣi) is Viṣṇvāditya, who presides over the state of consciousness (cittatva); the meter (chandaḥ) is Atyaṣṭī; the deity (devatā) is Kāmeśvara, whose body is adorned by Lalitā—the mother of the venerable Sekara situated in the Tāmasa-sukāra-pīṭha—and who is named Sarveśvara; [this is for] the attainment of all that arises.
The application.

Through the grace of the hymn of devotion, performed with body, senses, and mind, [the obstacles] become paralyzed; paralyzed, they reach a state of paralysis consisting of the cessation of their own functions. 4.
"Oṃ, obeisance to Tripurasundarī; Oṃ, obeisance to Tripurasundara," and so forth. 12.

Of this *Śrīsvāhānta-mithunamālā-mantra*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Brahmāditya, who presides over the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*); the meter (*chandaḥ*) is *dhṛti*; the deity (*devatā*) is the Lord Bhaṭṭāraka Karukarakaumeśvara, whose body is adorned by Lalitā and who resides at the Kāmaka-pīṭha within the letter *ka* of the *tāmasa* [category]; its application (*viniyoga*) is for the attainment of the goals of human existence (*puruṣārtha*).
O auspicious one, for you who are my devotee, there shall be the attainment of the three goals of life— dharma, artha, and kāma— which are immeasurable for embodied beings, without any effort.

Of this *mālā-mantra* of the Couple, ending with the venerable *tarpaṇa*, the seer (*ṛṣi*) is Nārāyaṇāditya, who presides over the principle of mind (*manas-tattva*); the meter (*chandas*) is *atidhṛti*; and the deity (*devatā*) is the Lord Kāmeśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, the leader of Kolāpura, adorned with the name Līlāvalī, residing upon the seat (*pīṭha*) of Tāmasarākāra.

O Devatā, this is the application for the attainment of eternal bliss; and the two types of supramundane countenances are not difficult to attain for those who cling to the lotus-feet of Paraśiva. 14.

33b) Of this *Śrījayajayātitamithunamālāmantra*, Rudrāditya, the presiding deity of the principle of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇatattva*), is the seer (*ṛṣi*); *prakṛti* is the meter (*chandaḥ*); and the venerable Lord (*bhaṭṭāraka*) residing at the *pīṭha* is the *hrīṃ* syllable of the *tāmasa* nature.
The deity named Hiraṇyeśvarī, whose emblem is adorned with Lalitā, and the venerable Kāmeśvara, who possesses much gold; this is the application for the attainment of liberation.
A deity who bestows worldly enjoyments is not conducive to liberation.
For this enjoyment, which bestows liberation, is the abode of the non-dual Lalitā. || 15 ||
Thus concludes the fifteenth garland: the meters, seers, deities, realities, meditations, and fruits. 4 kaṃ.

The seer (ṛṣi) of the syllable *ka* is Varuṇāditya; the metre (chandaḥ) is Gāyatrī. 4 Aiṃ. The seer of the syllable *e* is Mitraditya; the metre is Ullikh. 4 Īṃ. The seer of the syllable *ī* is Dhātāditya; the metre is Anuṣṭubh. 4 Laṃ. The seer of the syllable *la* is Aryamāditya; the metre is Bṛhatī. 4 Hrīṃ. [The seer] of the syllable *hrīṃ*...

Bhāskarāditya is the seer (ṛṣi), Paṅkti is the meter (chanda). 4. HŪM. For the letter *ha*, Aṃśāditya is the seer, Triṣṭubh is the meter. 4. SAṂ. For the letter *sa*, Bhagendrāditya is the seer, Jagatī is the meter. 4. KAṂ. For the letter *ka*, Vivaśvadāditya is the seer, Atigatī is the meter. 4. HAṂ. For the letter *ha*, Puruṣāditya [is the seer].

The Seer is Ṛṣi; the metre is Śakvarī. 4 Laṃ. For the letter *la*, the Seer is Bhāsvat; the metre is Atiśakvarī. 4 Hrīṃ. For the syllable *hrīṃ*, the Seer is Savitṛ Āditya; the metre is Yaṣṭi. 4 Saṃ. For the letter *sa*, the Seer is Viṣṇu Āditya; the metre is Atyaṣṭi. 4 Kaṃ. For the letter *ka*, the Seer is Brahmā Āditya; the metre is Dhṛti.
Chandaḥ 4 Laṃ: Nārāyaṇāditya is the seer (ṛṣi) of the syllable La, and Atidhṛti is the meter (chandaḥ). 4 Hrīṃ:
Rudrāditya is the seer (ṛṣi) of the syllable Hrīṃ, and Prakṛti is the meter (chandaḥ).
Thus ends the fifteenth chapter on meters and their seers.
Salutations to the form of the glorious Guru.
Sadāśiva, Īśvara, Rudra, Viṣṇu, Brahmā, and then Anākula;
Gaurīśa, Atrīśa, Mitreśa, Kapiṃlāṇḍa, and likewise Guru. || 1 ||
Siddhiśāsana, Piṅgākṣa, Manuṣyapuṣpadantaka,
Śāntayoga, and Tisra-saṃjña— these were his gurus in succession.
Vidyācārya, Vratācārya, Dūrvāsa, and Kaulika are considered [the teachers];
Jaigīṣavya is a Vratācārya, as is Kauṇḍinya Ācārya. (3)
And he who is known as Bhairavāṣṭaka, as well as Aṅgāraka and Guru;
Viśvanātha, Sāmeśa, Vasiṣṭha, and Viśvanāthaka. (4)
Gaṅgādhara, Guru, and Anantānandanātha;
[the name] Anantānanda follows from the word "Nātha" at the end of the title. || 5 ||

Each possesses their own power and union, with various mantras at the end of the words; all have hands in the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness, beginning with Śiva and following the lineage of one's own Guru.
Whoever recites the lineage of gurus (gurukrama) at the three junctions of the day endowed with faith,
for them there shall be infinite fruit from the rites of ritual placement (nyāsa), worship, recitation (japa), and so forth.
Thus ends the hymn to the lineage of gurus. Homage to the venerable gurus.
The venerable Guru, the Great Teacher (Mahācārya), the one to be worshipped by all, the Instructor;
likewise, the Lord Śrīnātha, the God, and the Great Bhaṭṭāraka. || 1 ||
He is the Great Lord, the Perfect Joy, the Lord of Yoga, as well as the one of great austerity; he is the Śrīdevī, the Kaulika, and the Avadhūtaka.
And "the Great Maheshvara"—these sixteen divine names of the illustrious Guru should be [recited] with devotion by the most excellent practitioner. (3)
At the commencement of learning, in rites for peace, or in rites for prosperity— at all times— a man,
having conquered with the sacrificial ladle, shall obtain everything he desires in every assembly.
Lions, rākṣasas, and others, as well as fevers, epilepsy, and harmful spirits, flee in great terror; this is the truth, the truth, there is no doubt. (5)
Thus ends the Śrī Guru Divya Nāma Stotra.
Salutations to the venerable gurus. Salutations to the Lord of the Gaṇas.
The Mālā-pancadaśā is proclaimed as the union of Śiva and Śakti;
it consists of the words "tarpaṇāt," "mahome," and the two words "namaḥ" and "jaya."
The Śivamālā is the first recitation; the Śaktimālā is the second;
and the Yugmamālā is the third here—thus the triad of fivefold groups is proclaimed.
Now, the fivefold Śivamālā is written: Oṃ Aiṃ Hrīṃ Śrīṃ. Of this Śrī Śivatarpaṇamālā mantra, Puruṣāditya, the presiding deity of the sense of touch, is the seer (ṛṣi).

The meter is Śakvarī; the deity is the venerable Kāmeśvara Bhaṭṭāraka, known as Kāpharavallabha, who resides at the Mokṣa Rājasahakāra Bhaṭṭāraka Pīṭha and is adorned by the beloveds of Hara; his application is for the accomplishment of all subjugation (vaśya).
Meditative absorption.
Having surrendered their body, wealth, and life like one's own servants,
those who serve you as your devotees become subject to you, O King.

One should perform the six-limbed rite with the *vālā* mantra; having performed the preparation of the *argha* water, one should invoke [the deity] with the *hṛllekhā* mantra and worship with the *mālāmantra*.
